response: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an architecture designed to improve the factual grounding and reliability of language models by using retrieved documents from a knowledge base as context for generation. A standard RAG pipeline involves collecting and preprocessing documents, splitting them into chunks, and retrieving relevant information to answer queries. This approach helps reduce hallucinations and improve traceability, making it particularly useful for document question-answering systems and enterprise knowledge bots.
retrieved_contexts: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly known as RAG, is a powerful architecture used to improve the reliability and factual grounding of language models. Instead of forcing the model to answer purely from internal memory, a RAG system retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge base and then uses those documents as context for generation. This approach is especially useful for domain-specific assistants, enterprise knowledge bots, and document question-answering systems. By grounding the answer in retrieved evidence, the system can reduce hallucination and improve traceability.

Production engineering often involves making careful trade-offs between quality, cost, and speed. Security and access control become essential when RAG is used in enterprise settings. Internal company documents may contain confidential information such as contracts, salaries, customer records, architecture diagrams, or strategic plans.

There are multiple chunking strategies used in modern RAG systems. Fixed-size chunking is the simplest method, where text is divided based on a fixed number of characters, words, or tokens. This approach is easy to implement and efficient, but it often ignores semantic boundaries.

This second-stage ranking is slower but more accurate, and it can significantly improve the quality of the final context passed into the language model. Evaluation is one of the most overlooked parts of building a RAG system. Many developers focus heavily on ingestion, embeddings, and model integration, but never properly measure whether the system is actually retrieving the right information.

A standard RAG pipeline consists of multiple stages. First, raw documents are collected from sources such as PDFs, websites, Word files, internal wikis, or databases. These documents are then cleaned and preprocessed to remove noise, normalize formatting, and extract useful textual content. After preprocessing, the documents are split into smaller chunks. Chunking is extremely important because large language models have token limits and retrieval quality often depends heavily on how well the text has been segmented. If chunks are too large, retrieval becomes noisy. If chunks are too small, important context may be lost.
